newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks rattled by fresh interest rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks rattled by fresh interest rate fears.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks were dragged lower Thursday by fears of an interest-rate rise as new data pointed to a stronger-than-expected economy.

At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was off 12.58 points at 5,864.78, pulling back further from Monday's record close of 5,889.20. In the broader market, declining issues led advances 12-8 on moderate volume of 221 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index was up 4.06 at 1,209.77, boosted by fresh gains in technology stocks. The American Stock Exchange index lost 1.66 to 564.99.

Analysts said blue-chip stocks were rattled by news that construction starts on new homes and apartments in August were the highest in nearly 2-1/2 years, providing more credence to expectations the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates at its policy-setting meeting next Tuesday.
The Commerce Department said the building rate increased 4.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.525 million units -- the highest rate since March 1994.

In another report, the Labour Department said the number of Americans filing initial claims for unemployment insurance edged lower last week. The claims fell to 2,000 to 329,000 in the week ended Sept. 14.

"The market had previously had that big unexpected gain, but with the release of the report on Tuesday morning (that the Fed was more seriously considering a rate hike), the music stopped," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
"Now there is a kernel of doubt about what will happen at the Fed meeting, so the sense is to sit on your assets, why get in trouble?," he said.
Meanwhile, high-technology stocks rose as the sector again benefited from Monday's bullish forecast by Intel Corp. about its quarterly profits.

"With the background for tech stocks looking brighter, inventory problems dwindling, and the Nasdaq has not matched the gains of the S&P and Dow, its a better environment," said Charles Pradillo, an analyst at Cowen & Co.
"Assuming a good market through the (November) election, I expect the Nasdaq to outperform the major averages," he said.
"Window-dressing," where portfolio managers buy into stocks in order to make their accounts look stronger at the end of the third quarter also featured in the market action.
In special situations, three initial public offerings were the highest-flying stocks on the Nasdaq.

Cymer Corp., a maker of excimer lasers for deep ultraviolet photolithography systems used in the production of the very small images in advanced semiconductor chips, jumped 3-7/8 to 13-3/8 in its Wall Street debut.
Rental Services Corp., which rents out pumps, generators, forklifts and other industrial equipment, rose 5-1/4 to 21-1/4, or 32 percent in its first day of trading.
Another IPO, RMH Teleservices, rose 3-1/2, or 28 percent, to 16.
Furniture company Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. rose 3 to 30-1/2 after it forecast strong profits for the latest quarter.
